items.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002
items.q: And well I had already met Horace Parlan but we worked together with Lou Donaldson and really became close.

ctx.x: I can remember being on the road with him and he’d come to my room in the morning while I was still sleeping, and he’d come in, “Well what did you do last night Jimmy Wormworth?” and blah, blah, blah. And we’d talk and he’d stand in front of me, he’d go to the dresser in my room and stand in front of the mirror and look at his embouchure. Just feel it and press it and examine it and look at it. And one of his idols was Johnny Hodges at the time, curiously enough. Charlie Parker was his main idol, but he loved

Johnny Hodges, I think for his tone. And tone was such a big thing to Lou. And he has such a great tone. And he used to be I think even bigger back then, but he worked on it so much. And he practiced long tones. He was — he taught me a lot. He tried to encourage me to concentrate more on playing the time, just playing the beat on the cymbal, and less on embellishing — comping as it’s called — with my left hand on the snare drum, commenting, filling in. “I’m going to tie your left hand behind your back.” I’d be…
Mingus pretty much taught Danny Richmond how to play didn’t he?
